text:
Last Wednesday I announced in the company Slack: from Q4 we collect transcripts of all calls. Even 1:1s. Even the ones with people partners.

— 𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘷𝘢𝘤𝘺? — the people asked. 
We are not machines producing corporate data. In a one-on-one, the work stuff inevitably mixes with the personal. If everything gets recorded, we will start filtering every phrase. AI will happily pull a thought dropped by accident out of context, turn it into an "objective signal," and neatly put it at the base of an evaluation, a promotion, or a firing. We don't know who gets access to this data, how long it is stored, or whether we can delete or correct anything. We will tell less truth, or just move the important conversations to where nobody records them. 😐

— 𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘦𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘺? — the business answered. 
For business, people are the data. We work in service, a devshop. We need to spot and promote the people who can communicate effectively, facilitate, build relationships, run retrospectives, and not be toxic. It is exactly these competencies that lead to client problems getting solved and to the client being comfortable. That is what he pays the money for. And hiring people just to fire them is dumb; business doesn't work like that.

Until AI showed up, a company under 100 people simply had no way to analyze the calls and behavior in them. And now, please: "𝘊𝘭𝘢𝘶𝘥𝘦, 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘳 𝘶𝘴𝘦𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘯 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬." Or "𝘧𝘪𝘯𝘥 𝘮𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘳𝘶𝘥𝘦." And there is your material for evaluating effectiveness. 👀

By the way, right now, evaluation in the company is built on the subjective opinion of people. That opinion quietly rests on the last two months of working together, because whatever happened before that, nobody really remembers anymore. A full transcript, on the other hand, keeps the phrase together with everything that was said around it. That is exactly what nobody has at hand when the argument about context starts. 

𝗦𝗼 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆, 𝗶𝘁 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗴𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝘂𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗯𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴.

And yes, the biggest fear — that I will be evaluated by AI — is the reality now. It will be.

So, dear managers, HR people, and everyone who has ever written a performance review, how do you evaluate people right now, and how much of it is just what you happen to remember? 🤔
